summary: This informational document proposes guidelines for considering human rights in protocol design, similar to the privacy considerations in RFC 6973. It explains the background and how the guidelines were developed, and is the first milestone of a longer research effort.

plainLanguage.summary: It asks people who design internet rules to stop and think about how their designs affect people's rights, such as speaking freely.

subtitle: A research group's attempt to link protocol design to human rights, and a questionnaire for protocol authors.

tldr.problem: Protocols are often seen as purely technical, yet their design choices can enable or restrict rights such as freedom of expression and association, and there was no shared way to think about that.
tldr.mechanism: The IRTF Human Rights Protocol Considerations Research Group reviewed the literature, analyzed RFCs, interviewed over 30 people and observed working groups. It then built a vocabulary, a threat discussion and a questionnaire of 19 technical concepts for document authors.
tldr.outcome: The guidelines do not recommend specific practices. They are a first milestone of a longer effort, and the RFC has been updated by RFC 9620.

facts.label: Published by
facts.value: IRTF Human Rights Protocol Considerations Research Group

today: RFC 8280 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 9620, which sets guidelines for human rights considerations in protocols and architectures. The RFC itself describes its work as the first milestone in a longer-term research effort.

sections.title: Why Protocols Matter for Human Rights
sections.content:
This document has three aims: to expose the relationship between protocols and human rights, to propose guidelines for protecting the Internet as an enabling environment for human rights in future protocol work (in the manner of the privacy considerations in RFC 6973), and to raise awareness in both the human rights and technical communities. Authors who only want to apply the work can go straight to Section 6.

The text argues that open, secure and reliable connectivity is necessary, though not sufficient, for rights such as freedom of expression and association. It also notes that rights can conflict, for example expression and privacy, so impacts need to be documented and balanced. It cites RFC 3935: 'The Internet isn't value-neutral, and neither is the IETF.'
sections.plainLanguage: The internet helps people talk and gather. This document says the people who build it should think about how their building choices affect those freedoms.

sections.title: Research Questions and Literature
sections.content:
The group set two questions: how can protocols and standards enable or restrict human rights, and can guidelines improve informed and transparent decision-making about that impact?

The literature review finds five positions on whether human rights belong in protocol design. Clark et al. argue for designing for variation in outcome, not hard-coding rights. Brown et al. argue that key universal values, with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the legitimate expression, should be built into the architecture. Broeders suggests treating the public core of the Internet as a common public good. Bless and Orwat say it is too early for definitive claims and more analysis is needed. Berners-Lee and Halpin suggest new capacities may over time be seen as new rights.

The research group's own position is that hard-coding human rights into protocols is complicated and changes with context, and that it is difficult to say whether it is wise or feasible. It does hold that conscious, explicit and documented design decisions are important.
sections.plainLanguage: Some experts say rules for the internet should have people's freedoms built in. Others say it is too early or that things should stay flexible. The authors say: at least think about it and write down your choices.

sections.title: How the Research Was Done
sections.content:
The method combines discourse analysis with ethnographic methods. The working idea is that the language in IETF and IRTF documents reflects how engineers understand their work. The group read RFCs, ran a Python-based analyzer (the Bigbang tool adapted by Nick Doty) to scan for architectural concepts, then did a qualitative pass to catch what word counts miss.

Data came from three sources: discourse analysis of RFCs and mailing lists, over 30 interviews at the IETF 92 meeting in Dallas in March 2015 with IAB and IESG members, working group chairs and RFC authors, and participant observation in working groups starting at IETF 91 in Honolulu.

The analysis mapped protocols to rights, extracted frequently occurring technical concepts, built a common vocabulary, and matched the components of rights to technical concepts. It also presents case studies such as IPv4, DNS, HTTP, XMPP, peer-to-peer, VPNs, HTTP status code 451 and DDoS attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The researchers read lots of old rule documents, counted key words with a computer, talked to many people who build the internet, and sat in on their meetings.

sections.title: Technical Concepts and Threats
sections.content:
The RFC groups technical concepts by the rights they can affect. Connectivity, privacy, security, content agnosticism, internationalization, censorship resistance, open standards and heterogeneity support are all tied to the right to freedom of expression. Other groupings cover non-discrimination, equal protection, political participation, cultural life and education, and freedom of assembly.

Section 6.1 describes threats. Protocols and standards can harm or enable the rights to freedom of expression, non-discrimination, equal protection, cultural participation, freedom of assembly and association, and security. A person whose communications are monitored may be kept from associating or taking part in political processes, and in the worst case protocols that leak information can lead to physical danger. The threat modeling is inspired by RFC 6973, and the RFC calls it imperfect but the best approach currently available.

The mapping is explicitly not complete or exhaustive; it is an initial set drawn from interviews and the literature.
sections.plainLanguage: Some design choices, like hiding who is talking or leaving content alone, protect people. Others, like leaking who is talking, can put them at risk.

sections.title: The Questionnaire for Protocol Authors
sections.content:
Section 6.2 gives a questionnaire with one entry for each of 19 concepts, from Connectivity and Privacy to Authenticity, Adaptability and Outcome Transparency. Each entry has questions, an explanation, an example, and the rights it can impact. It is not a checklist of required practices. The RFC says the range of IETF protocols is too broad to recommend particular practices, and that the aim is to support a documented discussion of whether a protocol adequately takes human rights threats into account.

For example, the Connectivity questions ask whether the protocol adds application-specific functions to intermediary nodes, using the end-to-end principle. The Censorship Resistance questions ask whether the protocol makes it apparent when access to a resource is restricted, and the example points to status code 451 from RFC 7725. The last item, Outcome Transparency, asks whether the effects of the protocol, including unintended consequences, are easy to understand.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of quiz questions for people making new rules, like 'could someone use this to block messages?' and 'could this reveal who is talking?'.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section says that because the document discusses research, there are no security considerations. The IANA section says the document requires no IANA actions. The practical effect is that the document gives no new protocol requirements. It only offers questions for authors to apply to their own work.
sections.plainLanguage: Because this document is about ideas and not a new machine, there is nothing new to lock up or register.

viz.caption: FIVE ACADEMIC POSITIONS REVIEWED IN THE RFC

items.title: Clark et al.
items.text: Design for variation in outcome; do not hard-code rights.

items.title: Brown et al.
items.text: Bake key universal values, such as the UDHR, into the architecture.

items.title: Broeders
items.text: Treat the public core of the Internet as a common public good.

items.title: Bless and Orwat
items.text: Too early for claims; analyze design impact more carefully.

items.title: Berners-Lee and Halpin
items.text: New capacities may in time be seen as new rights.
